content.title: WEIRD BODY GLITCHES THAT ACTUALLY MEAN YOU'RE MISSING {{A NUTRIENT}}
facts: **Restless legs at night** – that crawling, twitchy urge to move your legs right as you try to fall asleep can point to low **iron**, especially if you also feel colder than everyone else in the room.
**Cracking at the corners of your mouth** – small painful splits there often trace back to low **zinc** or **B2/B12**, not just dry weather.
**Muscle cramps that hit at night** – sudden calf or foot cramps while you sleep are a classic low **magnesium** and **potassium** combo.
**White spots on your nails** – scattered white marks across the nail plate are commonly linked to low **zinc**.
**Bleeding gums when you brush** – gums that bleed easily, even with gentle brushing, can signal low **vitamin C**.
**Bone or joint aches with no injury** – unexplained deep bone pain, especially in the hips or lower back, is a known sign of low **vitamin D**.
**Dry eyes and trouble seeing at night** – struggling to adjust when lights go dim can point to low **vitamin A**.
**Numb or tingling fingertips** – a pins-and-needles feeling in your hands, not from sitting wrong, often ties back to low **B12**.
**Brittle hair that snaps mid-strand** – hair that breaks instead of stretching can reflect low **iron** or low **omega-3**.

content.caption:
A few of these are easy to brush off, but they're worth paying attention to. Take restless legs at night: low iron lowers dopamine activity in the brain, and dopamine is what keeps those leg-movement signals calm — so when iron drops, your legs get twitchy right as you're trying to wind down. Cracking at the corners of your mouth happens because zinc and B2/B12 are needed to repair the thin skin there; without enough, that tissue breaks down faster than it can heal. And those white spots on your nails show up because zinc plays a role in how nail cells form as they grow out from the base, so a dip in zinc gets "recorded" in the nail over weeks. Everyone's body is different, so take these as prompts to look closer, not a diagnosis.
